video:video.video:title: 1Password Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the polished, category-leading pick, and it's priced like it — free and cheaper managers exist, so you're paying for the UX, ecosystem and business controls, not raw functionality. For a business, that's usually worth it.

video:video.video:title: AWeber Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free and low tiers are generous, but Lite and Plus prices climb with your subscriber count, so budget for growth. It's a dependable, no-frills veteran — just not the most modern automation on the market.

video:video.video:title: ActiveCampaign Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pricing climbs with contact count and the add-ons (CRM, SMS, extra seats) stack up fast — the sticker Starter price is not what a serious automation setup actually costs. Powerful, but budget for the tier (Plus and up) you'll really use.

video:video.video:title: Adwisely Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest math is the 10%-of-ad-spend fee on top of the minimum. It is cheap at low spend, but at higher budgets it's a real percentage cut of your marketing dollars until the cap — so calculate the effective cost at your actual spend, not the $49 sticker. It's built for e-commerce retargeting/prospecting on Meta and Google specifically, so it's not a general campaign manager. For stores that want largely hands-off retargeting, it removes real work.

video:video.video:title: AfterSell Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Post-purchase upsells only move the needle with steady order volume and a sensible complementary-offer strategy — bolt it onto a store with little traffic and there's nothing to upsell. The no-rev-share model is a genuine plus over percentage-based rivals.

video:video.video:title: AhaSlides Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: AhaSlides runs regional pricing: the number on the pricing page depends on where you browse from — so any review quoting one price (including ours) may not match yours. The advertised savings assume annual commitment, and the free tier's five-quiz-slide cap nudges real quiz use toward paid.

video:video.video:title: Airwallex Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest headline here is that the FX markup is published at all — 0.5% and 1% above interbank is a real number, and most competitors will not print one. What the page does not settle is everything around it. The Grow plan's platform fee 'varies with team size' with no table, so the $12 a user is not the whole subscription -- though their table does say the first ten Spend users are free, which is the part the headline rate hides in your favour. Chargeback and dispute fees are not priced anywhere, only mentioned as a feature. And the page's own disclaimer says per-transaction fees apply to certain transactions with the detail in a separate fee schedule. So: use the published FX rate to compare against your bank, then ask for the fee schedule and the platform fee before you move money.

video:video.video:title: Algomo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Algomo is a member of the quote-only club: $200/month is the only number on the site, and the real bill for your traffic volume and feature set only emerges in a sales conversation. Budgeting before the demo is guesswork — and quote-priced tools rarely get cheaper at renewal. Worth knowing before it becomes load-bearing: the personalisation runs from a JavaScript snippet in your header, so the tailored copy and routing rules live for as long as the subscription does. Remove the snippet and every visitor sees the original page again.

video:video.video:title: Alidrop Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Alidrop's pitch includes faster-shipping (including US/EU) suppliers, but the core dropshipping economics still apply: you pay the subscription plus wholesale product cost, and margins live or die on product selection and ad efficiency, not the tool. The low Starter product cap nudges serious stores up to Pro quickly, and as with any dropshipping automation, the platform reduces but doesn't remove supplier-quality and shipping-time risk. Sample before you scale.

video:video.video:title: Alli AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry is $299 a month — agency-grade automation priced accordingly — and every tier meters on FOUR axes at once (sites, seats, keywords, pages), so growth on any axis forces the upgrade. And the category caveat an honest review owes you: bulk automated on-page edits are powerful, but changes at scale deserve human review — unchecked automated SEO is how sites break. One more thing the pricing page does not answer, and it matters at $299 a month: where changes are delivered through that snippet rather than written into your CMS, they last exactly as long as the subscription does. Price this as renting an improvement, not buying one, and ask them directly what happens to applied changes after you cancel before you commit a year to it.

video:video.video:title: Alohi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that Alohi is a suite of separate products — Fax.Plus, Sign.Plus, Scan.Plus — each with its own subscription, so "one ecosystem" can mean several line items if you want e-signatures and faxing and scanning. Page and member limits on the lower tiers are modest, and HIPAA/BAA sits only on the top tier. For a single job (say online faxing), it's clean and cheap; for the full workflow, add up the parts.

video:video.video:title: Alvys Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest boundaries. Implementation can stretch into weeks and support is ticket-based rather than real-time — a real friction in trucking's tempo. And it's built specifically for truck-based FTL operations: if you're a pure-play (non-asset) broker, run LTL with multiple customers per load, or need rail/air/ocean tracking, this isn't your TMS — Alvys itself is refreshingly explicit about that. The fit is narrow and deep, not broad.

video:video.video:title: Amplitude Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Unlimited seats is genuinely unusual and worth the credit — you are not taxed for letting the whole team look. The cost lands on events instead, and events are the thing you control least: an instrumentation change or a growth spurt moves your bill without anyone choosing to upgrade. The page gives no rate per event beyond the free 2 million, only an estimator, so you cannot work out what 20 million events costs without entering the funnel. And 'expanded packages are priced as a percentage of your platform plan' means the add-ons scale with your bill rather than with your usage of them — the more events you send, the more the extras cost, whether or not you use them more. Get the per-event rate in writing before you instrument.

video:video.video:title: Apollo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The credit and export caps are the catch — real usage on enrichment and dialing often runs well above the sticker, and data accuracy is hit-or-miss, so verify before you outreach at scale.

video:video.video:title: Aspire Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a fintech account (strongest in Southeast Asia), not a full bank — great for keeping fixed costs near zero on mostly-domestic activity, but confirm it supports your country and currencies before you build your finances around it.

video:video.video:title: Audiorista Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $29 Demo tier cannot actually publish to the App Store or Google Play — real branded apps start at $240 a month. The Business tier adds a per-active-user fee from $0.80 on top of $400 per app, so growth literally raises the bill — and Apple and Google's own store commissions still apply to in-app sales on top of everything.

video:video.video:title: Aura Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tier is decided by how much you sell, not by what you need. That is unusually honest as a model — a seller doing $10K a month is not subsidising one doing $900K — but it means your bill moves when your business does, in the same month, without you choosing to upgrade. Pass $15K and Starter stops being the plan you are on. Work out which band you land in the way the page measures it: their table says monthly sales are calculated on a trailing two months, so it is a sustained climb rather than a single spike that moves you up. Two smaller things: the marketplace count is a real cap (two on Starter, so Amazon plus one), and the AI listing allowance is per listing rather than per repricing action, so a large catalogue eats it faster than a busy one.

video:video.video:title: Auware Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's deliberately narrow — Shopify-only and built around segmented paid traffic. If you send everyone to one page or don't run audience-segmented ads, the core 'a page per persona' value doesn't really kick in. It's also newer and less battle-tested than general builders like PageFly.

video:video.video:title: BabyLoveGrowth Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest concern here isn't the price — it's the model. Auto-publishing 30 AI articles a month and building $800+ in backlinks monthly is exactly the scaled-content-and-links pattern Google's spam policies (Helpful Content, link-spam) are written to catch. It can lift metrics short-term; on a brand you're building for years, it's a real durability risk. The 90-day money-back guarantee is a genuine plus that offsets some of that.

video:video.video:title: Barcodes Talk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest caveat is about fit, not the codes. Some large retailers and brand registries — notably certain Amazon Brand Registry and big-box requirements — increasingly ask for a GS1-issued prefix tied to your own company, and a third-party barcode (legitimate and globally unique as it is) may not satisfy that specific gatekeeping. For most marketplaces and independent retail it's completely fine and far cheaper; just confirm your channel's exact requirement first.

video:video.video:title: Beautiful.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The smart-template engine is the feature and the fence: decks look polished with zero design skill precisely because the system constrains you, so pixel-perfect custom layouts and heavy brand exceptions fight the tool. And note the billing gap — $14.50/mo annual becomes $45 month-to-month, one of the steeper monthly premiums around. If your organisation lives in PowerPoint workflows, test the import/export round-trip before committing.

video:video.video:title: Beefree Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the seat row before the price row. Professional and Business both cap at two full editing seats, so a "mid-sized team" plan at $134/mo annual still buys two people who can actually build. Everyone else lands in view-only slots — four on Professional, ten on Business — or an Enterprise quote. The free Starter is the odd one out: unlimited users, but with no roles or permissions at all. Exports are metered at six a month, rather than the unlimited free tier its old reputation suggests. And the naming is a live tripwire. Since 14 May 2026 the builder is RGE Studio at reallygoodemails.com, while Beefree remains the company name and the name of the separate developer SDK. So check which product a plan or invoice actually refers to. It is purely a creation environment that never sends, so it always sits on top of your ESP. Worth it when the ESP's native editor is the bottleneck — agencies, multi-brand teams, ESP migrations — and duplicated effort when it isn't.

video:video.video:title: Beehiiv Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Next to Substack it's more to learn. Substack's built-in discovery network and dead-simple setup are easier if you're starting from zero with no audience and don't care about automation or SEO. Beehiiv's depth is the point, but it's a steeper start.

video:video.video:title: BillingNow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is genuinely refreshing — two plans, same features on both, unlimited users, no per-seat maths. The honest watch-out is the trial length rather than its terms: three days is short for migrating billing into a new tool, and the practical constraint is that there is no import path. The help centre documents CSV and Excel export but no import, so an existing client list has to be retyped — which is more than three days of work for anyone with a real book. It is also a young product from a small Geneva maker, so weigh ecosystem depth and longevity before you move your billing history in.

video:video.video:title: Birch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that pricing tracks your ad spend. The tidy $49/$99 tiers assume you stay under a $10k monthly ceiling, and past it you either pay spend-based overages or move to custom Enterprise — so a scaling advertiser's real cost rises with their budget. It's also a power tool: rule-based automation across Meta, Google, TikTok and Snapchat rewards advertisers who know what to automate, and can amplify mistakes if your rules are wrong. For hands-on performance marketers, it's a serious time-saver.

video:video.video:title: Bitdefender Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Like most antivirus, the first-year price is a promo — renewals run notably higher, so budget for the renewal rate, not the intro. It's consistently top-rated on protection, so the real trade-off is cost, not efficacy.

video:video.video:title: Bokun Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bokun is a Tripadvisor/Viator company, and that's both the draw and the lock-in. Distribution to Viator and 2,600+ resellers is excellent, but you're building your booking backbone inside one OTA's ecosystem, and the per-booking service fee on direct sales is a real cut on top of the subscription. If most of your business is direct, weigh that fee; if you live on OTA distribution, the Viator advantage is hard to beat.

video:video.video:title: Bolt Business Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest boundary is geography: Bolt's network is Europe/Africa-centric across 600+ cities, so US-only operations should look elsewhere, and ride availability varies by city — pilot it on your team's actual routes. Pricing is dynamic like all ride-hailing; the business layer adds control and receipts, not fixed corporate fares, so budget-predictability comes from your spend limits, not from locked prices.

video:video.video:title: Bookyourdata Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The model is honest — no subscription, credits keep, bad data refunded — so the real scrutiny belongs on usage. Bought lists are only as good as your targeting and your sending infrastructure, and cold-emailing purchased contacts has legal boundaries that vary by country, GDPR territory especially. The data being accurate doesn't make the campaign compliant; that part is yours.

video:video.video:title: Boulevard Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things about this price list. It is per location, so the arithmetic for a second salon is not a volume discount, it is double — and the add-ons are per location too, which compounds it. And every listed price is shown struck through against a higher 'normally' figure, footnoted on 18 August 2026 as a limited-time summer offer for new customers only. Treat the higher number as the list price a renewal may return to, and the lower one as an introductory rate with an end date you should ask about. The third thing is not a price at all: you cannot buy this without booking a demo. That is a signal about how the deal is done, and it means the published numbers are a starting point rather than a checkout.

video:video.video:title: Bread & Butter Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two meters to watch: it prices per WEBSITE (multi-site setups multiply the $49) and the AI features run on compute-credit blocks that stack as usage grows. On privacy, refined twice in open dialogue with the vendor (16 Jul 2026, verified against their docs). The anonymous journey IS tracked from the first visit, server-side via their site plugin. So ad-blockers and Safari’s ITP don’t strip it the way they kill client-side scripts — the vendor estimates 30-50% of high-value traffic is lost to client-side blocking. What stays dormant until someone submits an email is identity resolution — the ‘hand-raise’ that connects the captured history to a verified person. You still owe normal GDPR care on enriched data, and the real trade-off is simply this: no IP-based guessing at which company an anonymous visitor works for.

video:video.video:title: Breezy HR Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The jump from free (one position) to the first paid tier is steep if you only hire occasionally — the free plan is genuinely usable, so live in it until you're filling several roles at once.

video:video.video:title: Brevo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Charging by sends rather than contacts is genuinely cheaper for big lists you email infrequently — but the free daily cap and add-on fees mean high-frequency senders should model their real send volume first.

video:video.video:title: Bright Data Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is enterprise-grade web data infrastructure at enterprise-grade prices — the per-GB meter looks small until you multiply by real scraping volume, and the committed tiers only pay off if your usage is steady. The bigger honest note is compliance: Bright Data is strict about KYC and use-cases (a feature, not a bug), and whatever you collect still has to respect the target sites' terms and applicable law. Budget legal thought alongside the gigabytes.

video:video.video:title: Browse.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest realities of no-code scraping. Credits burn faster than expected: row counts, screenshots and 'premium' sites all multiply the meter, so monitor a big site daily and do the math first. And scrapers break when sites redesign — robots need maintenance, which is your time even when the tool is no-code. Also check the terms of the sites you monitor; 'technically possible' and 'permitted' aren't the same thing.

video:video.video:title: BuddyPunch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: That flat $19 base fee makes it pricey for very small teams — at three or four users the base fee dominates the bill, so it's better value once you're past a handful of employees.

video:video.video:title: Buzz.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two meters run at once: seats AND credits — the seat price includes a credit allowance (500 a month on Core, 5,000 on AI Employee, read 5 September 2026), and real outbound volume means credit packages on top, so budget past the sticker. Watch the moving numbers too: the page changed twice this summer — a $75 teaser, then $79 a seat; $795 with a promised rise to $1,000, then $695 — and the $2,500 setup fee now sits on Enterprise and the white-label plans, so decide on the total for the plan you are actually offered, not the sticker. And the honest fundamental for any AI-SDR: it only books meetings as good as your list and offer, so keep a human reviewing what goes out in your name.

video:video.video:title: CallRail Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline price is a floor, not a ceiling — the included minutes, numbers and SMS are modest, so an active campaign quickly hits metered overages that meaningfully lift the bill. It's also specifically an attribution tool: it proves which marketing drives calls and leads, but it isn't a phone system or CRM, so you add it alongside those, not instead of them.

video:video.video:title: Campaigner Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two paragraphs of fine print worth reading. Automation workflows and conversion tracking only arrive on Advanced (from $35 a month at 1,000 contacts) — Essentials is a sending tool with an API, not a marketing-automation platform — and the trial auto-converts to paid if you do not actively cancel, which tells you something about the retention strategy. Contact-based pricing also means dormant subscribers bill like active ones; prune first.

video:video.video:title: Carbon6 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest headline here is not pricing but ownership — and it has moved again, this time in the reader's favour. SPS Commerce bought Carbon6 for roughly $210M on 7 Feb 2025 and retired the brand into spscommerce.com. On 30 Jun 2026 it sold the entire 3P (Amazon marketplace seller) revenue-recovery business for $9.5M cash, booking an estimated $20M loss, and named no buyer at the time. There is a name now. The partner-programme notice we received on 17 Aug 2026, from Carbon6's own partnerships contact, states that SPS transferred ownership of the 3P business to Carbon6 and that commission terms and payouts are unchanged. It also states that existing links were redirected to the Carbon6 tool sites on 14 Aug 2026, and that the programme itself rebrands from SPS to Carbon6 on 24 Aug 2026. Reading carbon6.io on 17 Aug 2026 matches that: the whole suite is on sale there again as "by Carbon6". Read the two purchase numbers carefully, because they are not the same thing. The $210M bought the whole Carbon6 stack; the $9.5M was the 3P arm alone, and offloading it at a book loss seventeen months in still tells you how it performed. What remains undisclosed is who stands behind the Carbon6 entity itself, so the question is answered one level down and no further. Two more things to hold. Reuters reported on 23 Jun 2026 that SPS hired Morgan Stanley to explore a sale of itself under activist pressure, with talks early and no deal assured. And the 1P side is no longer a clean split, because SPS kept the deduction-recovery business it bought while Carbon6's own site now lists ChargeGuard for Amazon 1P vendor recovery. Ask which entity your 1P work would sit with before you sign. For 3P reimbursements the July advice has expired — you can name the counterparty on your contract again.

video:video.video:title: Checkr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The headline per-check price is rarely what you actually pay — passthrough fees vary wildly by county and search type, so budget for the effective cost, not the advertised one. It's overkill unless you hire at real volume.

video:video.video:title: Circle Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The sticker is only the entry: Circle keeps a commission on every sale on top of Stripe's processing fees, and email marketing is a separate add-on — so a monetized community's real bill runs meaningfully past the plan price. Model it at your actual sales volume before choosing a tier.

video:video.video:title: Claude Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is usage limits: even on Pro you can hit a ceiling mid-session on a heavy day, and the step up to Max is a real $100 to $200 a month — you're buying headroom, not extra features. It also doesn't generate images, so if that's your main need it's the wrong tool, and its third-party plugin ecosystem is smaller than ChatGPT's.

video:video.video:title: Clay Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest catches: a steep learning curve (expect 2–4 weeks, many teams need a dedicated Clay expert), and credits that are hard to forecast at scale. It's an enrichment engine, not a sender — you still need Instantly, Lemlist or Outreach to actually email.

video:video.video:title: ClickUp Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The everything-app breadth is also the downside — it's feature-dense with a real learning curve, and teams can drown in options. Powerful and cheap per seat, but only if you'll actually configure and adopt it.

video:video.video:title: Clonable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest caveats. First, it's a continuous subscription, not a one-time translation — you pay ongoing to keep the translated clone synced with your site. Second, it's machine translation under the hood, so quality varies by language pair; always have a native speaker spot-check high-stakes pages. (Public pricing was gated at research time — confirm current tiers yourself.)

video:video.video:title: Clutch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's genuinely free to submit a brief — but be clear on what it is: a lead-generation marketplace, not a neutral directory. Your brief goes straight to agencies who will reach out to pitch you, and providers pay to be visible and matched. It's a fast way to shortlist vetted agencies; just expect the outreach that comes with it.

video:video.video:title: Cognism Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: No price, no credit allowance, and a five-seat minimum on both named plans. That combination means the smallest deal is five seats of something you cannot price, so budget conversations start with a sales call rather than a number. The credit model is the part to nail down: one credit reveals one contact, so your real cost per usable lead is the credit price divided by your connect rate, and neither figure is published. Before the call, work out how many contacts a month you actually reveal — that is the only number that lets you judge the quote you get. And it is worth asking whether unused credits roll over, because nothing on the page says.

video:video.video:title: Connecteam Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free-for-10 plan is one of the most generous in the category, but the three-hub structure means costs can stack if you need all of them — price the specific hubs you'll actually use, not the full bundle.

video:video.video:title: Consensus Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It searches peer-reviewed literature, which is its strength and its boundary: it can tell you what published studies found, not whether those studies are good. Study quality, sample sizes and conflicting results still need your judgment, and the AI summary layer can smooth over genuine scientific disagreement. Treat it as a dramatically faster literature scan, not an oracle; click through to the papers that matter.

video:video.video:title: Contractor Foreman Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credit where it is due first: this is company pricing with unlimited projects and no per-user overage inside your tier, which is rare in construction software and genuinely cheaper than per-seat rivals for a crew. The catch is the billing term. Quarterly costs 26% more than annual on the same plan — $132 against $105 on Standard — and Basic is not sold quarterly at all, so the cheapest way in requires a year paid up front. The user counts are the real ladder: 1, 3, 8, 15, unlimited. A five-person crew is not on Standard at $105, it is on Plus at $166, so count your licence holders before you compare against anything else.

video:video.video:title: Convert Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is tested users, and it keeps running: blow past your monthly allowance and overuse blocks land at $399-699 unless you hard-cap them — and every extra custom domain is $1,000 a year. The friendly $299 headline assumes annual prepay; month-to-month is $399. One thing people misprice, and it is not the test itself: everyone expects an experiment to end when the subscription does. The trap is the winner. Convert describes itself as a client-side tool where “adding just one snippet of code on your site will then do all of the magic”. So a winning variant you leave running in the visual editor is not a change to your site — it is a rendering by their script. Ship the winner into your own code, or you are paying rent on a result you already bought.

video:video.video:title: CrankWheel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's deliberately narrow — instant, no-download screen sharing for sales calls — so it's excellent at that one job and thin everywhere else: no full video-conferencing suite, no deep collaboration or webinar tooling. Mind which plan caps what: the free plan drops to 15 sessions a month after the first fortnight and Team puts everyone on a shared pool of 100, while Solo is the one paid tier with unlimited usage. If you want an all-purpose meeting platform, this isn't it; if you want prospects to see your screen in seconds with zero friction, that focus is exactly why it works.

video:video.video:title: Credit Repair Cloud Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is business-in-a-box software for starting a credit-repair company, not a tool that repairs your own credit — the price only makes sense if you're actually building a client business on it. The middle tiers jump fast as you add clients and seats, and success depends far more on your sales and compliance discipline (credit repair is a regulated space) than on the software. Buy it as an operator, not a consumer.

video:video.video:title: CrowdStrike Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two numbers decide whether this is for you, and neither is the headline. The first is the 100-device ceiling on Falcon Go: it is not a soft limit you grow through, it is the point where you change product. The second is the annual rate, which is worth doing the division on — $59.99 a year against $7.99 a month is $95.88, so annual saves 37%, one of the larger annual discounts in security software. Beyond that, be honest with yourself about which tier you are comparing: Go is antivirus with a good agent, and the endpoint detection and response that CrowdStrike is famous for starts at Pro. Comparing Go against a full EDR product from a competitor is comparing the wrong things.

video:video.video:title: Databox Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing model bites: Pro connects only 3 data sources, so the per-source fees stack up fast — and for agencies juggling many clients with diverse tools it gets expensive. Power users may also find the custom-metric and data-modelling depth limited next to a full BI tool.

video:video.video:title: Deputy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The minimum monthly spend is the number to check before anything else: at $5.50 per user on monthly billing, a team of fewer than about six people still pays the $30 floor, so the headline per-user price is misleading at small scale. Beyond that, the plan you probably want is not the one you first price — auto-scheduling, demand forecasting and labour budgets sit in Core, and SSO, custom access levels and location hierarchies only in Pro, which has no public self-serve checkout. The add-ons stack per user as well, and the payroll add-on is US-only and annual-only.

video:video.video:title: Descript Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's per-editor pricing with two meters running underneath: media hours AND monthly AI credits. Heavy podcast or video volume burns through the caps fast, and the free tier watermarks 720p exports — model your real production hours before picking a tier. The API changes the arithmetic rather than escaping it. Their own API page states access is included for paying users at no additional cost, but the work it does draws from the same AI credits and media minutes — so automating a pipeline burns the caps faster, not slower. It also stops just short of the finish — the same page says direct media file exports are not supported yet, so the export step stays a manual one in the app. (read on their own API page, 2026-08-14)

video:video.video:title: Devs.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is the smaller half of the bill. Personal includes $10 of usage a month and Business $21, with model usage metered on top of the seat. The plan cards state the included amount without stating the rate you pay once it runs out — which is exactly the number you need to forecast a real workload. The free plan is a demo rather than a working tier: both builders are limited to "Core", and workflows, APIs and integrations are absent entirely, which is much of what would make the platform useful past a first agent. And for a product sold on IT governance, the governance controls are the ones you cannot buy with a card — SSO, access control lists and white-labelling sit on the Enterprise tier, behind a custom annual contract.

video:video.video:title: Dify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Free' self-hosting isn't free — you own the servers, updates and reliability, and model usage bills separately once the included message credits run out. Dify Cloud takes that infrastructure work off your hands, but every cloud plan is a single workspace, and multiple workspaces, SSO and a commercial licence sit in quote-only Enterprise. It's powerful, but self-hosting it well needs technical comfort.

video:video.video:title: Diginius Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: All-in-one marketing dashboards live or die on data depth per module. Diginius bundles PPC, SEO, lead intelligence and reporting affordably, but specialists — a dedicated SEO suite, a dedicated PPC optimizer — go deeper in their lanes. So buy it as consolidation for a lean team, not as a replacement for expert-grade tooling in your primary channel. Verify the integrations you depend on (especially Microsoft Ads, its historical strength) in the trial.

video:video.video:title: DropGenius Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: We have to be blunt here: DropGenius carries a very poor Trustpilot rating (around 1.6/5 at research time), with recurring complaints about charges continuing after cancellation and refund difficulty. An AI-generated store in 30 seconds is also just a starting template — the product selection, marketing and margins remain entirely your problem. If you proceed: pay attention to cancellation mechanics from day one, screenshot everything, and treat the Renewal Radar as mandatory equipment.

video:video.video:title: Dryground AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is consulting, not a tool you log into: best when you want AI designed and built for you, not when you'd rather DIY with software. Read the headline numbers carefully too. The 20-50% efficiency and 10-20% revenue figures on their homepage carry the caption “2025 industry benchmarks”, so they describe the market rather than this firm's own results. And the case studies underneath them name no clients.

video:video.video:title: EasyDMARC Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You are buying domains and history, not features. Plus covers two domains; a company with a main domain, a marketing subdomain and a legacy domain it forgot about is already over. And the history window is the part that bites later: three months on Plus means that when you are investigating a spoofing campaign that started in the spring, the reports are gone. The page also does not say what happens when you pass the message volume. Their own FAQ does: you lose access to your reports and dashboard rather than being billed for overage. That is a harsher failure mode than an overage charge, and worth knowing before you size the plan.

video:video.video:title: ElevateForward Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a strategy-to-execution layer, not a task app or a dashboard — so the value only lands if leadership actually adopts the framework. 'Operational alignment platform' is also a fuzzy, crowded label, so press them on the concrete deliverables (the diagnostics, KPI blueprints and execution plans) before committing.

video:video.video:title: ElevenLabs Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credits are the meter and retakes are the tax — you are charged per generation request, and a regeneration is only free while the content and settings are unchanged, so real usage lands well above the calculator estimate. And read the free-tier fine print: $0 gets you 10k credits to play with, but no commercial license — anything you publish commercially needs at least the $6 Starter. Voice realism genuinely leads the market; niche names and jargon can still need manual retakes, so run your hardest paragraph through the free tier before subscribing.

video:video.video:title: EmailListVerify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $5 entry pack is the most expensive way to buy: $0.005 per check versus $0.00196 at the 50k tier — a 2.5x spread that rewards guessing your volume upfront. And the email finder quietly consumes 5 credits per found address, so a 1,000-credit pack finds 200 emails, not 1,000.

video:video.video:title: Emergent Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The real cost is credit consumption, not the flat sticker -- a genuinely complex app burns 10-20+ credits per big change, so serious builders move up tiers faster than the price list implies. Now do the division, because Emergent's own pricing page doesn't. Standard is $20 for 100 credits, so 20 cents a credit. Pro is $200 for 750, which is 26.7 cents. Moving up a tier makes every unit of work more expensive, not less: Pro costs 33% more per credit than Standard, and annual billing keeps the gap (17 cents against 22.3). That is the opposite of the volume discount the ladder looks like -- you are buying a 1M-token context window, custom agents and priority support, not cheaper work. And there is nowhere cheap to go above it: Business and Enterprise are both quote-only, so passing 750 credits a month means a sales call rather than a bigger plan. Check what your month actually needs before you upgrade; one Standard month plus purchased extra credits may beat one Pro month. AI-generated code still needs a human eye: review it for security, correctness and maintainability before anything touches real users.

video:video.video:title: EngageBay Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is contacts AND seats at once: prices are per user, and each tier caps contacts — Basic’s 500 contacts fills fast, and the Growth jump is steep ($15 → $65 per user). The advertised ‘starts at $12.74’ assumes biennial prepay — two years upfront for the friendly number. Real automation only starts at Growth.

video:video.video:title: Envoy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: None of the prices on that page is a price you can budget from. Four of the five product cards are followed by 'Price excludes platform fee', and the platform page says outright that the platform is required to use Envoy products and is charged as a flat annual fee — with its own Premium and Enterprise tiers to pick first, and no number published anywhere. That is the first thing to ask for. The second is how the meters stack, because they are all in different units: per location, per user, per bookable resource, per device, per delivery location. An office with forty bookable desks, six screens and one delivery point is paying on four clocks at once: $362 for the location, $200 for the desks, $72 for the screens and $250 for deliveries. That is $884 a month before the platform fee, and before emergency notifications at $2 a head. Price the combination you actually want, not the product you came for.

video:video.video:title: Evolve Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's built for large organizations — the site lists 100+ deployed enterprises like Carlsberg and Danone — and the sales-led, quote-only motion reflects that: there is no self-serve tier to trial quietly, so smaller teams can't just kick the tires before procurement gets involved.

video:video.video:title: Expertise AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is that there is no middle any more. When we re-read the pricing page on 15 August 2026, the $500/mo Growth tier had been withdrawn. So the ladder runs straight from a Free Preview capped at 10 conversations to Business at $2,000/mo. And everything that makes the product genuinely powerful — visitor intelligence that de-anonymizes traffic, the 2-way HubSpot sync, Voice AI — sits on that paid tier. There is no way to grow into it gradually. It's also a RAG agent, so it's only as good as the docs you feed it: give it thin content and it can answer buyers confidently but wrong. Strong for HubSpot-centric B2B teams; less compelling if you're not in that ecosystem.

video:video.video:title: Fastmail Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You're paying for what the free giants monetize differently: no ads, no profiling, real support and standards-first email (JMAP/IMAP everywhere). The honest limits: it's email/calendar/contacts, not a Workspace-style office suite, so document collaboration lives elsewhere, and migrating decades of Gmail habits (filters, integrations) takes a weekend of care. For owning your address on your own domain, it's the boring, excellent choice.

video:video.video:title: Feedvisor Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest structure: the $100 tier is a limited on-ramp, and most of what Feedvisor is famous for (the algorithmic Buy-Box strategy that holds prices UP, ad management, analysts) lives behind the $1,500+ top tier — this is enterprise software for serious catalogs, priced accordingly. If your Amazon revenue can't absorb that as a small percentage, simpler repricers are the rational choice.

video:video.video:title: Finale Inventory Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's built for real warehouse volume and priced that way: Essentials starts at $499 a month and Growth at $799, with Enterprise quoted. There is no self-serve tier and no published order or user cap -- every plan goes through Request a Demo, most customers sign 12- to 36-month terms, and API and EDI access are Enterprise-only. If you do a few dozen orders a month, this is far more inventory engine, and far more cost, than the job needs.

video:video.video:title: Fireflies.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The advertised $10 and $19 are annual-billing rates; month-to-month is $18 and $29. And AI credits are capped on every tier — Pro carries the same 20 a month as the free plan, so upgrading to Pro buys recording and storage rather than more AI. If you mainly want real-time in-Zoom captioning and simple English notes, Otter is the simpler pick.

video:video.video:title: FlexiQuiz Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The monthly response caps are the business model: 20 on free, 500 on Essentials, 2,000 on Premium and 25,000 on Enterprise -- one viral quiz or one big exam cohort and you're shopping a tier up. The per-response price falls steeply as you climb ($0.034, $0.0125, $0.0024 on yearly billing), so the ceiling is the thing to price, not the sticker. Administrator seats are capped separately at 1, 2 and 15, and sharing a login is against the terms.

video:video.video:title: Flippa Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The real cost is the success fee, and it's a flat bracket rate on the whole sale price, not marginal — a mid-five-figure sale can hand over a four- to five-figure commission. Flippa is also a self-serve marketplace: more listings, but more due-diligence burden on you. Verification and quality vary, so buyers must vet hard and sellers should expect tyre-kickers. It's reach and liquidity, not a white-glove broker.

video:video.video:title: Flocksy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Unlimited' means unlimited queue, not unlimited throughput: work happens at your plan's daily capacity, so a big launch week still needs planning, and turnaround expectations are where subscription-design relationships sour. The economics are simple and honest — against even one freelance designer's day rate, the math works IF you feed it steady volume; if your design needs are sporadic, a flat monthly fee is paying for silence — unused hours do bank, but only for 30 days.

video:video.video:title: Foxit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Foxit's pitch is being the honest fraction of Acrobat's price, and on the headline numbers it delivers. The catch used to be that e-signing was always a second subscription. As of our 28 August 2026 reading that is only true below Editor+, which now includes Foxit eSign with 150 envelopes a year. The trap has moved rather than gone: buy the $129.99 Editor, then find you need signatures, and Editor plus standalone eSign Essentials is $249.99 a year against $159.99 for the Editor+ that bundles it. AI is still an add-on at $49.99 a year beyond the 300 monthly credits, and it is not sold for perpetual licences at all. Price the basket, not the first line.

video:video.video:title: Frase Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The article quotas pinch if you publish at volume (overage docs bill each), and it's a research-and-optimization tool, not a magic ranking button — it speeds up briefs, it doesn't replace the writing or the backlinks.

video:video.video:title: Freshchat Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is genuinely useful for small teams, but AI features and higher-tier routing sit behind paid plans and add-ons — and being part of the wider Freshworks suite means you'll be nudged toward the full platform.

video:video.video:title: Freshservice Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $19 headline rarely survives contact with a real deployment: the ITSM features most IT teams buy for (change/problem management, deeper analytics) live at Pro, and the modern extras — AI agent sessions, orchestration runs, asset counts — meter separately. Price the tier that contains your must-haves plus realistic AI usage, not the starter row. Within that honesty, it's one of the fastest ITSM tools to actually stand up.

video:video.video:title: FullEnrich Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pay-on-success model is refreshingly honest, but note the 10x: phone numbers eat credits ten times faster than emails, so a calling-heavy motion consumes budget quickly — model your email/phone mix. As an orchestration layer over 15+ providers, its hit rate genuinely beats single databases; the flip side is you're paying a premium per contact versus querying one source that might have sufficed.

video:video.video:title: Gamma Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The credit model means heavy generation eats your monthly allowance, and outputs still need a human polish for high-stakes decks — it's a brilliant first-draft engine, not a finished-deck button. The free tier's watermark pushes you to paid quickly.

video:video.video:title: Gelato Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is genuinely usable, so the honest question is only whether Gelato+ earns its fee — and that depends entirely on volume: below ~10 orders a month the discounts won't cover the subscription. Its real edge is local production in 30+ countries (fast, cheaper international shipping), but that means quality and product availability can vary slightly by region and print partner. Sample your key products before scaling.

video:video.video:title: Geotargetly Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is pageviews, not visitors, and each product consumes its own pageview on the same page visit — so a redirect plus a popup bills twice. Run out and you get two days to upgrade or re-subscribe before services stop. The friendlier advertised numbers are the yearly rates; month-to-month runs about 25% higher. And the dependency worth pricing in: the rules run from a script you drop into your site, so they exist only while that script is served. Stop the subscription and every visitor sees the same page again, wherever they are.

video:video.video:title: GetResponse Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Priced by contact count, so the entry number climbs as your list grows, and the best value only shows on long (annual/24-month) commitments. A solid all-rounder, but you lock in to get the good rate.

video:video.video:title: Getscreen Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: AnyDesk tends to feel faster and lower-latency, and TeamViewer carries the heavier security/compliance certifications (HIPAA, SOC 2). Getscreen's real edge is being fully browser-based — nothing to install on the other person's machine — and cheaper, especially with the lifetime deal.

video:video.video:title: Goflow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every tier ships the whole platform — you pay for volume, not unlocks — and Core really is free forever, so 500 orders a month costs $0. The catch is the cliff above it: orders past the Core allowance are paused until you upgrade, and the next step up is $499/mo. Goflow also states you cannot move back down to Core once you go paid. Budget the EDI setup separately: $500-1,300 one-time per connection, multiplied by the number of retail partners.

video:video.video:title: Gorgias Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Never priced per agent is a real advantage and worth saying plainly: your whole team can be in the inbox without the bill moving. The cost sits on two meters instead, and both bite. Tickets beyond your allowance are $0.40 each, so a bad week costs money rather than attention. And the AI agent — the thing the homepage leads with — is a separate $30 a month on the entry plan, which is three times the helpdesk it sits on. Automated interactions past 30 are charged at $1.50 each. So the honest entry price for the product as advertised is $40, not $10. Count a normal month's tickets and a busy month's, and price both.

video:video.video:title: Guesty Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pricing runs higher than leaner rivals, onboarding has a learning curve, and some users flag support — it earns its keep at scale, but it's heavy for a single listing.

video:video.video:title: Healthie Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest limits: it's pricier than alternatives with thin mid-tier options, and several users report slow customer service (sometimes a week or more to reply). It really only pays off at scale — solo or tiny practices get more value, more simply, elsewhere.

video:video.video:title: Hello Bar Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is views, not results: every visitor who sees a popup counts against your quota, so a traffic spike raises the bill regardless of how many emails you actually captured — a busy site outgrows the entry tier fast. And the honest fundamental of every popup tool: it amplifies an offer, it doesn't create one. A weak lead magnet with a beautiful popup is still a weak lead magnet, and aggressive full-screen takeovers can cost more goodwill (and Core Web Vitals) than they capture.

video:video.video:title: HiBob Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Opaque pricing and an implementation fee mean the real cost only surfaces in a sales call — and it's built for scaling mid-size companies, so it's heavy and expensive for a small team.

video:video.video:title: Hive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is honest bait, the add-on grid is the business model: switch on three add-ons and your $12 seat becomes $27 — a la carte flexibility that punishes teams who need the full toolkit. List your must-have modules first and compare the DRESSED price against all-inclusive rivals; for teams needing only core PM, though, Hive is genuinely cheap and pleasant.

video:video.video:title: Hopp Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest note is that the platform is free and the rides are not. Hopp Business charges no activation fee and no minimum commitment, so the whole cost is ride pricing, which moves with city, vehicle class and demand — and coverage thins out wherever Bolt does not already run. Check both on your own routes before you move a travel budget across.

video:video.video:title: Housecall Pro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The Basic tier is a trap for real field teams — it omits GPS tracking and QuickBooks sync, so most businesses need Essentials or up. And the seats are the expensive part: users beyond the five on Essentials cost $100 a month each ($75 on MAX), on top of card processing quoted as 'as low as' 2.59% and a 1% fee on bank payments. Price the tier and the headcount you'll actually need.

video:video.video:title: Hubstaff Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat definition is the whole story and they state it plainly, which deserves credit: you pay for every seat you have created, not every person actually being tracked. So an account that grew with your headcount and never got tidied up is billing you for people who left. Audit your seat list before renewal, not after. The second thing is that features on the lower tiers are add-ons rather than inclusions — Insights, Tasks, Silent app and extra screenshots at $2.50 a seat a month, Locations at $3.33 — so the plan you priced and the plan that does what you watched in the demo may differ by ten dollars a seat. And be clear with yourself about why you are buying it: screenshots and activity levels change how a team feels about their work, and that cost does not appear on any pricing page.

video:video.video:title: IDrive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The first-year price is a teaser and the renewal is the price — IDrive says so itself under the plan table, and on the current numbers the step from discounted to standard is about 43% (Personal 5 TB goes from $6.99 to $9.99 a month). Budget on year-two rates, not the banner, and note that the discount is for new signups only and not available through their mobile apps. Overrun your storage and there is a further $0.25/GB/month on Personal, $0.50 on Team and Business. Beyond that, the honest backup fundamentals apply: a backup you never test-restore is a hope, not a backup, and the first full backup of multi-TB data takes weeks over the wire unless you use their physical Express seed shipping.

video:video.video:title: InVideo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest catch is the credit model — each plan is a fixed monthly credit allowance that different models consume at different rates, and unused credits do not roll over, so a heavy month can exhaust an allowance long before it renews while a slow month simply wastes what you paid for. There is also no free way in any more: on 31 August 2026 the pricing page published no free tier at all, so the cheapest route to trying it is the Plus plan at $20 a month. AI video is fast but generic by default: templated output needs real editing and brand direction to not look like everyone else's. Treat it as a first-draft engine, not a finished-studio replacement.

video:video.video:title: InboxAlly Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is a premium, seed-list-based deliverability tool, and the price reflects it — Starter alone is well above casual warm-up apps, so it only makes sense if inbox placement is genuinely costing you real revenue. It improves sender reputation through engagement signals, but it's not a magic fix for bad content or a purchased list: deliverability still depends on how you actually send. Buy it when the math (lost revenue from spam-foldering) clearly beats the monthly fee.

video:video.video:title: Increff Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is enterprise omnichannel supply-chain software, and the opaque, quote-based pricing signals the target customer: retail brands with real scale, not small stores. The value — algorithmic merchandising and inventory optimization — only pays off at a catalog and volume large enough for those optimizations to move money. For a small or mid seller, it's likely more platform (and cost and implementation) than the problem warrants. For a scaling omnichannel brand, it's built for exactly that.

video:video.video:title: Insightful Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is employee-monitoring software, so weigh the culture cost, not just the price: the advertised $8-16 rates are per seat AND assume annual billing, security features like insider-threat detection are a paid add-on, and monitoring tools can damage trust if rolled out without transparency.

video:video.video:title: Instapage Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's premium-priced and only justified by serious ad spend — Create is $79 a month billed annually for 15,000 unique monthly visitors, and the price per thousand barely improves as you climb, so the higher tiers buy features rather than cheaper traffic. The 14-day trial needs a card and carries its own cap of 2,500 visitors; crossing it ends the trial and starts the paid plan by itself. And there's the ownership question the feature list does not raise: publishing to your own domain means pointing a CNAME at Instapage — their help centre carries a per-registrar guide for exactly that — so the page is served by them and lives as long as the subscription does. Their own docs add a second catch worth knowing before you standardise on it: “we lock domains under the first Instapage account that uses them”. Treat these pages as rented campaign infrastructure, not as part of your site, and keep the copy somewhere you control.

video:video.video:title: Jibble Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Free forever with unlimited users is a real claim and unusual in this category, where per-seat pricing is the norm — that alone makes it worth a look for a team on a tight budget. Two things to establish before you rely on it. First, what the free tier actually excludes, because 'unlimited users' and 'unlimited features' are different promises and the paid tiers exist for a reason. Second, note that their pricing page leads with a calculator showing what you supposedly save rather than what you pay. That is a marketing choice, and the number it produces rests on assumptions about payroll leakage that are theirs, not measured in your business.

video:video.video:title: Jotform AI Agents Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The gating detail is conversations, not features — Starter's 100 a month is a few days on a live site, and an agent that actually gets used will push you up a tier. Sessions are metered separately and Jotform counts a chatbot view or a page refresh as one, so a busy page burns allowance without ever holding a conversation; voice minutes and SMS meter on top as well. It's also tightly bound to the Jotform ecosystem: brilliant if you already live in Jotform forms, less compelling as a standalone chatbot if you don't. For form-driven support and lead capture, it's a fast, low-code win.

video:video.video:title: Jubilee Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a focused vertical tool — bankruptcy petition preparation and case management — so its whole value is bounded by that practice area; a general legal practice won't get much from it. The case-count tiers are the thing to size correctly: pick 36 vs 300 by your real annual filing volume, and check whether the pay-per-case option is cheaper if you file sporadically. For a bankruptcy practice, the automation and court-form handling are exactly the point.

video:video.video:title: Kartra Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: If your core need is polished course delivery, Kajabi's creator features are stronger; Kartra wins on all-in-one breadth, not course depth.

video:video.video:title: Katana MRP Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $299 headline is the floor. Production routings and traceability are paid add-ons on top, and those are exactly the features most manufacturers need, which is why real bills often land two to three times higher. Cost also rises with sales-order volume, so a busy month is a bigger month. It's genuinely capable manufacturing software; just price the add-ons you need, not the base plan.

video:video.video:title: Keap Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Cost is the big one (56% of reviewers flag it), the interface feels dated, and there's a real 2–4 week learning curve on the automation builder. Billing and cancellation complaints are common — their own terms carry a $299 early termination fee on an annual contract and require ten days' phone notice — and email design is thinner than dedicated email tools.

video:video.video:title: Kinsta Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You're paying a premium for managed speed, Google Cloud infrastructure and expert support — worth it if performance and hands-off management matter, wasteful on a low-traffic hobby site a $5 shared host would carry fine.

video:video.video:title: Landingi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You trade away the high-end optimisation: no AI traffic routing like Unbounce's Smart Traffic, no real-time collaboration, and thinner technical control (script containers). Excellent value, but not the conversion-optimisation powerhouse.

video:video.video:title: Leadpages Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the value pick, not the optimisation pick — if you're spending big on ads, Unbounce's Smart Traffic and Instapage's 1:1 personalisation go deeper.

video:video.video:title: LettrLabs Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Direct mail only pays off with a tight list and a real offer — it's a leverage channel, not a cheap thing to test blindly.

video:video.video:title: Lindy.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Cost tracks headcount rather than output: every colleague who so much as @mentions Lindy in Slack takes a paid seat, and a seat you remove runs to the end of the cycle with no mid-cycle proration. Credits are published now, but as ranges: an everyday ask is 2-250, a big build 1,000-2,500. So a month is still an estimate. And when the shared pool runs dry there is no top-up — Lindy pauses credit-using actions until the reset, unless an admin moves the workspace to a bigger plan.

video:video.video:title: Livestorm Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is a bet on attendance that you place a year in advance. You buy credits up front — €2.50 each in euros, $3.00 in dollars, set separately rather than converted — and a credit is spent per unique participant per session, so a four-part series to the same 200 people is 800 credits, not 200, which is €2,000. A webinar that does better than expected runs you out, and the page is now clear about what that means: new attendees cannot join until you buy a higher tier. The page publishes the per-attendee rate but never a total. Before you commit, count sessions times expected attendees for the whole year, and ask what happens to unused credits at the twelve-month mark, because the page does not say.

video:video.video:title: Logome.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Update, 6 Sep 2026: logome.ai no longer answers at all. Every route — homepage, pricing, app, dashboard, robots.txt, sitemap.xml — returns Webflow's default 404, and there is no app subdomain: app.logome.ai does not resolve in DNS. Our July note said the public site was down but the app still loaded; that is no longer the case. Treat every figure below as last-known rather than confirmed, and if you are already paying, cancel through your card or PayPal rather than through a site that will not load. The honest catch, when the service was reachable, was the free-to-design, pay-to-download model, with the entry tier giving one file without a transparent background. AI logos are also a starting point rather than a trademark: check distinctiveness before you build a brand on one.

video:video.video:title: MRPeasy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Paying ~$50 per user just so a shop-floor worker can clock in and out feels steep when they'll touch a fraction of the features. Customisation and reporting are limited, and there's no advanced demand forecasting or AI — so larger or highly complex manufacturers will outgrow it.

video:video.video:title: ManyChat Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Flows are button-and-script based, not natural language — type something unexpected and the bot falls back. The AI add-on is closer to keyword-matching than real conversational AI, billing scales with contacts (a viral Reel can spike your bill), and support is email-only and slow.

video:video.video:title: MarketerHire Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is expert freelance talent at expert prices — the value is speed and vetting (their pricing page promises a match within 24-48 hours, against a months-long hire), but it is a real five-figure-a-month commitment for serious engagements, not a cheap gig marketplace. Because it's talent, not software, outcomes depend on the individual and how well you brief them; the rematch guarantee helps, but you still own the strategy. Right when a great marketer would pay for themselves, wrong as a budget stopgap.

video:video.video:title: Marketing 360 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest cautions. Pricing is hidden and quote-driven, and reviewers repeatedly flag that the real cost — software plus design plus managed services — climbs well above the headline, sometimes with recurring fees for features you don't use. And it's an all-in-one "we'll do it for you" model, which is great if you want a single vendor and a human team, but it can mean less flexibility and more lock-in than assembling best-of-breed tools. Ask exactly what's included before signing.

video:video.video:title: MeetGeek Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is transcription hours and Pro gives you twenty a month, which is about an hour a working day. That sounds generous until you count the meetings you would actually record — a sales rep on four calls a day passes it in the first week, and the overage is $0.50 an hour. Unlimited transcription is the real reason to be on Business at $17, so treat Pro as a plan for occasional recording rather than a cheaper version of the same thing. Worth checking before you buy: consent. A recorder that joins every meeting changes what people say in them, and that is a policy decision rather than a pricing one.

video:video.video:title: MindStudio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The no-markup model pass-through is genuinely fair — but it also means your real cost is subscription PLUS model spend, and an agent that loops or processes big documents burns provider credits invisibly until you set limits. The honest build discipline: start every agent with usage caps, and treat 'no-code' as no-code for the plumbing — the logic design and prompt quality are still entirely on you.

video:video.video:title: Miro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-member pricing charges for every member added to the workspace, so an org-wide rollout multiplies at full headcount — and the free plan's 3-board cap is workspace-wide, not per person, so real teams outgrow it in days. Model who truly needs to edit before you buy seats.

video:video.video:title: Mktg.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest cautions. First, the price is still hidden — a 404 where the pricing page should be, and no pricing item in the navigation — which for a tool that promises spend transparency is an irony worth noticing, and the FAQ makes it sharper: its own introduction says it covers what the platform costs, and then no answer in it names a figure. What the FAQ does publish is the tier names, Growth and Enterprise, and the fact that EU data residency is Enterprise-only. Second, the ROI story is the vendor's own: the homepage tile assumes a $5M budget and puts a 3% efficiency gain at $150K alongside $100K of reallocated spend, which is 2% of the same budget. Ask for verified case numbers at your spend level on the demo call.

video:video.video:title: Momence Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 'free' plan is the most expensive one once you have real volume: a 5% commission on every sale overtakes Pro's $60 flat fee around $29k a year in processed revenue, and Pro in turn loses to the $199 Custom plan above about $67k a year. Pick your tier by volume, not by sticker — and note what the middle tier does not include. The tooltip on the Pro card lists the same exclusions as the free plan: no add-ons, no phone number, no inbox, no retail products, no reporting or insights, no staff members, no locations. Pro halves your commission and adds no features.

video:video.video:title: Moosend Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The friendly $7-9 headline is the entry rate at the smallest list size (500 contacts), and the ladder above it does not fall smoothly: paid annually, 8,000 contacts costs $51 a month while 10,000 costs $70, so a list of 9,000 sits on the wrong side of the sharpest jump on the slider. The same reversal repeats at 100,000 and at 600,000. Read the comparison table before you assume Pro covers you, too: transactional emails, SSO and SAML, a dedicated IP, hosted files and an account manager are Moosend+ add-ons or Enterprise rather than included.

video:video.video:title: Murf Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is generation hours per YEAR, not per month — 24 hours sounds generous until you count retakes, and regenerating a script three times bills three times. Voice quality is genuinely strong, but the honest test for any TTS is your specific language, names and jargon: generate your hardest paragraph in the trial before subscribing, because demo voices always sound better than your edge cases.

video:video.video:title: NordVPN Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: For a business you're really buying NordLayer, priced per user with a seat minimum. It's solid and easy, but a VPN is one layer of security, not a whole strategy — don't mistake it for endpoint protection.

video:video.video:title: Notify Me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It does one job — turning out-of-stock moments into recovered sales via back-in-stock and pre-order alerts — and its value is entirely tied to how often you actually sell out. If your catalog rarely goes out of stock, you won't see much return. As with any Shopify app it's another monthly line item and another script on your storefront, so weigh it against the real revenue you're leaking to stock-outs.

video:video.video:title: Omniseo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest cautions. AI search visibility (GEO) is a young, fast-moving category. Tracking how you appear in ChatGPT and other AI answers is genuinely useful signal, but the metrics are far less standardized than classic SEO — and you're paying to monitor a moving target you only partly influence. And the step from Essentials to Professional is a big jump for more channels and prompts. Treat it as an early-mover intelligence tool, not a guaranteed ranking lever.

video:video.video:title: Oneflow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry is €250 a month on annual billing — €3,000 a year committed before you've sent your first contract — and the rest of the ladder lives in a sales conversation. If you only need documents signed, dedicated e-sign tools start at roughly a tenth of that.

video:video.video:title: Outgrow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two meters at once: content types and pieces gate the lower tiers, and monthly LEAD limits gate the upside. Read the caps rather than the prices — Freelancer Limited allows 250 leads a month, Freelancer Pro 1,000, Essentials 7,500 and Business 50,000 — because per lead, Essentials and Business cost almost the same and the real jump in value is from Pro to Essentials. Also note what money does not fix: Outgrow's branding stays on every plan below Essentials, comes off there only under the small-business programme, and a custom domain is Business-only at $600 a month. Interactive content genuinely converts better than static forms, but only when the calculator or quiz gives real value; a thin quiz wrapped around a lead form fools nobody.

video:video.video:title: Ownr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest limits. It's Canada-only — provincial incorporation covers Ontario, Alberta, BC and Quebec — so it's no use outside Canada. And it's built for straightforward setups: it won't handle complex share structures, multi-investor shareholder agreements, tax planning, partnerships or non-profits. For those you still want an accountant or lawyer.

video:video.video:title: PDWare Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is genuine enterprise software with enterprise buying: opaque pricing, demo-first sales and implementation effort — appropriate for portfolio offices planning hundreds of resources, overkill below that. The honest pre-purchase question is organizational: resource-first planning only works if your PMO will actually maintain forecasts; the tool formalizes discipline, it can't create it.

video:video.video:title: Pangram Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The unavoidable honest limit of every AI detector, including accurate ones: it is never infallible. It will occasionally flag genuinely human writing as AI (false positives) and miss some AI text, so it must be used as a signal, never as sole proof for high-stakes calls like academic penalties or hiring. Pangram's pitch is fewer false positives than rivals, which is real progress — but 'fewer' is not 'none'. Pair it with human judgment and the credit meter with your actual volume.

video:video.video:title: Papaya Global Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every headline price is a 'starting from' that dead-ends at 'book a demo'. And multiple reviewers report the real bill runs bigger than the sticker: 30-50% over quote, with setup, FX and filing fees surfacing after signing (reviewer reports, not universal terms). The documented contract is typically a two-year agreement with a rolling 90-day termination clause, so read the term and exit clauses closely before signing. The deeper structural knock is where the work happens. Outside the countries where Papaya owns entities, it delivers EOR through in-country partners; a third-party estimate puts the owned count near 40, and Papaya does not disclose which are owned versus partner. So at 15+ countries you're often one escalation removed from whoever actually runs your payroll. Clients report a recurring set of problems: invoicing errors, data that doesn't sync between Papaya and the partner, and missed or late payroll runs. Support decays from a named account manager into a rotating ticket queue with no live channel.
